inlines.text: 今天，我们宣布对提供商路由算法进行自 OpenRouter 成立以来最大的一次升级。

blocks.text: 此前，我们的默认路由器主要只奖励提供商一件事：低价。新路由器奖励的是真正对你最有利的推理：便宜，同时还要快、吞吐量高、可靠。能提供更多价值的提供商会自动赢得更多流量，因此每个提供商都有动力持续改进。这意味着你通过 OpenRouter 获得的推理会越来越快、越来越可靠、越来越划算，而你一行代码都不用改。

blocks.text: 它已经见效了。新算法带来了显著改善：TTFT 提升 16.9%，吞吐量提升 16.3%，容量错误大幅减少 67%！而成本仅小幅上升 6.0%。这还是在提供商尚未有时间针对新算法进行优化的情况下取得的。更多细节请查看完整的实验结果。

blocks.text: OpenRouter 上的大部分流量（约 77% 的请求）流向由多个提供商提供的模型。当请求没有包含明确的排序或提供商列表时，我们需要选择一个提供商来发送请求。此前，我们几乎完全根据输入 token 价格做出这一选择。提供商越便宜，获得的流量比例就越高，任何失败的请求都会被重新路由到下一个最便宜的选项。

回退机制能捕获失败，但用户要一直等到回退完成，而且速度上的改进得不到奖励。
该算法对实时性能变化视而不见，因此提供商必须退化到被完全降级的地步，才会反映在流量分配中。
提供商赢得流量的唯一方式就是降价，这迫使它们减少对确保可靠性和质量的基础设施的投资。
我们用来排名的价格几乎全是提示词输入价格，因此提供商可以通过奇怪的定价组合来保住流量份额，比如列出人为压低的输入价格，然后用定价过高的缓存 token 或补全 token 来弥补差价。

blocks.text: 新算法：针对一个好的回答“成本”几何进行优化

blocks.text: 新的路由算法会持续监测每个供应商的表现，据此计算出一个实时的路由成本，用来衡量用户为得到一个好答案要付出多少代价。路由成本包含三部分：实际花费的美元金额、等待响应所耗的时间成本，以及供应商失败或返回不可用响应时重试的成本。

blocks.text: 对于每个请求，路由器会根据该模型近期的流量，估算它会用到多少输入和输出 token。这个估算同时决定了一次尝试的两部分成本：你要付的价格和你要等的时间。

inlines.text: 对于每个请求，路由器会根据该模型近期的流量，估算它会用到多少输入和输出 token。这个估算同时决定了一次尝试的两部分成本：你要付的价格和你要等的时间。

blocks.text: 有效价格是供应商实际会向你收取的价格，根据近期实测流量计算得出。它反映了供应商真实的缓存命中率，以及模型输入与输出 token 的平均构成，因此可能与标价相差很大。这样一来，供应商就无法靠压低输入价格、把昂贵的缓存 token 或输出 token 藏起来的方式抢流量。

blocks.text: 吞吐量是与价格相互权衡的因素：更快的供应商可以收费更高，仍然能赢得你的请求。它的衡量方式是端到端的每秒输出 token 数，因此包含了首 token 时间，以及供应商流式输出完整响应所需的时间。路由器会按每个模型设定的换算比率，把这段等待时间折算进路由成本，换算依据是该模型各供应商的典型收费和速度。

blocks.text: 首 token 时间（TTFT）是指从发出请求到响应开始流式输出之间你要等待的时长。尽管它已经计入吞吐量，路由器仍会单独把它加进路由成本，因为交互式使用最依赖这一项。在智能体会话中，模型可能连续发起多次工具调用，每一次都要等待首 token。

blocks.text: 速率限制（HTTP 429）意味着供应商容量已满，拒绝了你的请求。你要先等到这次拒绝，然后整个请求才会转给另一个供应商。路由器会把这段等待时间加上一笔惩罚计入该供应商的路由成本，并按它触发速率限制的频率加权，所以影响通常不大。反复出现的速率限制，更多是通过下文所述的流量上限和退避机制产生影响。

inlines.text: 速率限制（HTTP 429）意味着供应商容量已满，拒绝了你的请求。你要先等到这次拒绝，然后整个请求才会转给另一个供应商。路由器会把这段等待时间加上一笔惩罚计入该供应商的路由成本，并按它触发速率限制的频率加权，所以影响通常不大。反复出现的速率限制，更多是通过下文所述的流量上限和退避机制产生影响。

blocks.text: 为了衡量新路由算法的影响，我们不能只做标准的 A/B 测试，因为路由行为的变化很难与控制组隔离开来。举例来说，如果新算法能更好地把流量从表现不佳的提供商那里引开，那么旧算法发往该提供商的请求就会发现可用容量更多、速度更快，从而让结果失真。请求形态和流量模式的巨大差异让难度进一步加大。单个“鲸鱼”用户如果针对某个提供商发起一连串自动化的高负载请求，无论我们用哪种算法路由，都会人为抬高该提供商的指标。

blocks.text: Today we’re announcing the biggest improvement to our provider routing algorithm since the founding of OpenRouter.

inlines.text: Today we’re announcing the biggest improvement to our provider routing algorithm since the founding of OpenRouter.

blocks.text: Until now, our default router mostly rewarded providers for one thing: a low price. The new router rewards the inference that is actually best for you: cheap, but also fast, high-throughput, and reliable. Providers that deliver more value automatically win more traffic, so every provider has a reason to keep improving. That means the inference you get through OpenRouter keeps getting faster, more reliable, and more cost-effective, and you don’t have to change a line of code.

blocks.text: It’s already working. The new algorithm has unlocked significant improvements in TTFT (16.9%), throughput (16.3%) and capacity errors (a remarkable 67% reduction!), with only minor increases in cost (6.0%). That’s before providers have had any time to optimize for the new algorithm. See our full experimental results for more details.

blocks.text: Where we were: the limitations of Price-Only Routing

inlines.text: Where we were: the limitations of Price-Only Routing

blocks.text: Most traffic (~77% of requests) on OpenRouter goes to models served by more than one provider. When a request doesn’t include an explicit sort or provider list, we need to pick a provider to send it to. Until now, we made that choice based almost entirely on input token price. The less expensive a provider was, the greater percentage of traffic it would receive, and any failed request was re-routed to the next cheapest option.

inlines.text: Most traffic (~77% of requests) on OpenRouter goes to models served by more than one provider. When a request doesn’t include an explicit sort or provider list, we need to pick a provider to send it to. Until now, we made that choice based almost entirely on input token price. The less expensive a provider was, the greater percentage of traffic it would receive, and any failed request was re-routed to the next cheapest option.

blocks.text: This price-only approach got users the lowest prices in the ecosystem, but it created some unintended consequences:

inlines.text: This price-only approach got users the lowest prices in the ecosystem, but it created some unintended consequences:
Cheap won even when it was bad.
Fallbacks caught failures, but users waited through them, and speed improvements weren’t rewarded.
The algorithm was blind to real-time performance variations, so a provider had to degrade to the point of being de-ranked entirely before it was reflected in traffic distribution.
The only way for providers to win traffic was to cut price, putting pressure on them to reduce their investments in the very infrastructure that ensures reliability and quality.

The price we ranked by was almost all prompt input price, so a provider could keep traffic share with weird pricing cocktails like listing an artificially low input price and then making back the difference with overpriced cached or completion tokens.

blocks.text: We wanted to ensure a marketplace where competing providers won traffic by serving better inference, not just cheaper inference.

inlines.text: We wanted to ensure a marketplace where competing providers won traffic by serving better inference, not just cheaper inference.

blocks.text: The New Algorithm: optimizing for what a good answer “costs”

inlines.text: The New Algorithm: optimizing for what a good answer “costs”

blocks.text: The new routing algorithm constantly monitors the performance of each provider to calculate a real-time Routing Cost that captures what a user pays for a good answer. The Routing Cost encompasses the price in actual dollars and cents, the cost of time spent waiting for a response, and the cost of retries when a provider fails or provides an unusable response.

inlines.text: The new routing algorithm constantly monitors the performance of each provider to calculate a real-time Routing Cost that captures what a user pays for a good answer. The Routing Cost encompasses the price in actual dollars and cents, the cost of time spent waiting for a response, and the cost of retries when a provider fails or provides an unusable response.

blocks.text: To put it simply: what does one try cost, and how often does it work?

blocks.text: For each request, the router estimates how many input and output tokens it will use from the model’s recent traffic. That one estimate sets both parts of a try: the price you would pay and the time you would wait.

blocks.text: Effective price is the price that the provider would actually charge you, calculated from recent measured traffic. It reflects the provider’s real cache hit rate and the model’s average mix of input and output tokens, so it can differ a lot from the list price. This ensures that a provider can’t win traffic by hiding expensive cached or output tokens behind a low input price.

blocks.text: The router prices your request at each provider’s effective price, and prioritizes the cheapest options.

inlines.text: The router prices your request at each provider’s effective price, and prioritizes the cheapest options.

blocks.text: Throughput is what trades off against price: a faster provider can charge more and still win your request. It’s measured as output tokens per second end-to-end, so it includes the time to first token plus the time it takes the provider to stream the entire output response. The router adds that wait to the Routing Cost using a conversion rate set per model, based on what its providers typically charge and how fast they are.

blocks.text: Time to first token (TTFT) is how long you would wait before the response started streaming. It adds to the Routing Cost on its own, even though it already counts toward throughput, because interactive use depends on it most. In an agent session, the model may make many tool calls in a row, and each one waits for a first token.

blocks.text: A rate limit (HTTP 429) means the provider is out of capacity and turned your request away. You would have to wait for the rejection, then your full request would go to another provider. The router adds that wait plus a penalty to the provider’s Routing Cost, weighted by how often it rate limits requests, so the effect is usually small. Repeated rate limits matter more through the traffic caps and backoff described below.

blocks.text: A failed try still costs its price and its wait, so the Routing Cost calculates the expected cost of having to retry until one works. If 1 in 5 tries fails, you pay for 1.25 tries per good answer.

blocks.text: A reliability error is a request that fails because of the provider. You would lose the attempt and have to retry, so each error carries a heavy penalty in the Routing Cost.

blocks.text: Sending every request to the single best provider would overload it, so traffic is shared. Faster providers can carry a higher Routing Cost and stay competitive. Everything inside the competitive edge shares most of the traffic, and being a little behind the best costs a little. Past the edge, traffic share drops off fast.

blocks.text: In order to measure the impact of the new routing algorithm, we had to go beyond a standard A/B test, because changes in routing behavior can’t easily be isolated from the control group. For example, if the new algorithm did a better job of routing traffic away from a struggling provider, the old algorithm’s requests to that provider would find more capacity available and get faster, skewing the results. Further compounding the difficulty is the enormous variability in request shape and volume patterns. A single whale user that spins up an automated flurry of high effort requests to a single provider can artificially inflate the metrics for that provider regardless of which algorithm we used to route their requests.

blocks.text: So we ran a switchback experiment: We split each day into 3-hour blocks and flipped each matched pair of blocks between the new and old router, with a one-hour burn-in period of discarded data each changeover, and measured the per-model impact across a representative sample of open source models over one full week.
